### Observed differences

- In the later window, A37 receives a clearly larger share of A32's outgoing transitions — about 35 in 100, up from about 21 in 100 — while the shares going to A36 (about 29% down to 22%) and A39 (about 29% down to 22%) shrink, and A38 slips from about 22% to about 19%. [DIR001]
- In the later window, A36 routes to A33 much more often (about 59 in 100 transitions, up from about 40) and to A37 much less often (about 38 in 100, down from about 58). [DIR002]
- In the later window, A37 routes to A36 more often (about 60 in 100, up from about 42) and to A33 less often (about 37 in 100, down from about 58). [DIR003]
- A36 now typically sits two event positions after A32 (about 59 in 100 cases, up from about 42) rather than immediately after it (about 39 in 100, down from about 58). [LAG001]
- A33 now typically sits immediately after A36 (about 60 in 100 cases, up from about 41) rather than two positions later (about 38 in 100, down from about 59). [LAG002]
- All five differences are unusually large for random re-splits — each exceeds the difference seen in about 199 of 200 reference comparisons — and each rests on roughly 100 to 200 observations. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, LAG001, LAG002]
- Secondarily, the observation volume behind the A36 and A37 profiles grew (outgoing transitions 99 to 119 and 98 to 116), hinting these activities ran in somewhat more traces; a few new destinations (A08, A17, A24, A10) appear on only one or two transitions each. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that the ordering around A36 and A37 reversed: in the earlier window the most frequent transitions read A32 → A36 → A37 → A33, with A33 two positions after A36, whereas in the later window they read A32 → A37 → A36 → A33, with A33 immediately after A36. This is an order hypothesis, and it is shown directly by relational and positional evidence that all points the same way: A32 now leads to A37 more often and to A36 less often, A37 now leads to A36 more often and to A33 less often, A36 now leads to A33 more often and to A37 less often, and both position gaps (A32–A36 and A36–A33) shifted by one step in the matching direction. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, LAG001, LAG002]

The routing and gap items describe the same small cluster of activities and likely the same traces, so they corroborate but do not independently confirm one another; the shift is also a redistribution rather than a complete rewiring, since A32 still goes directly to A36 in about 22% of its transitions and A36 still goes to A37 in about 38%, and the rare new edges rest on only one or two observations. An important competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is that both orderings already existed and only their frequencies shifted between the two 200-trace samples — sampling differences in variant frequencies could contribute to the pattern, although the size and consistency of the shifts make pure sampling noise unlikely. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003]
